paragraph.text: "cruelty-free" usually means only that the product and its ingredients weren't tested on animals. A product with that label can contain ingredients that come from the exploitation and killing of animals, such as carmine, lanolin, beeswax, honey, collagen, keratin and shark-liver squalene. So, in practice, cruelty-free isn't free of cruelty. Since 2025, Brazilian law bans testing cosmetics on vertebrate animals, as the European Union has done since 2009 (and since 2013 it has also banned selling cosmetics tested on animals), so "not tested" is becoming the minimum. Anyone who wants to avoid exploitation needs to look for products that are both vegan and not tested.

The bunny on the package means nobody tested that product on animals, and that's good. But the lipstick or cream can still have things taken from animals, like beeswax or a dye made from insects. To be sure, it's good to look for the vegan label too.

It's a good start, but check what the label says. Cruelty-free usually means only that the product wasn't tested on animals. It can still contain carmine, made from killed insects, lanolin, from sheep's wool, beeswax, collagen and keratin, from slaughtered animals, or shark-liver squalene. Not testing is an important step, and in Brazil it became law in 2025. But if you really want to avoid funding exploitation, the product also needs to be vegan. Otherwise, the animal stops suffering in the lab but goes on dying to become an ingredient.

text.bold: 1. The label is about testing, not ingredients.

paragraph.text: Certifications such as Cruelty Free International's Leaping Bunny deal with animal testing; they don't restrict animal-derived ingredients. A certified shampoo can contain keratin, lanolin or honey.

text.bold: 2. Many ingredients come from the exploitation and killing of animals.

paragraph.text: Skin, bones, hooves and feathers of slaughtered animals
Several of these ingredients also have plant or synthetic versions, and only the label or the brand can say which was used.

text.bold: 3. Not testing has become the legal minimum in several places.

paragraph.text: Brazil's Law 15,183 of 2025 bans testing cosmetics, hygiene products and perfumes on live vertebrate animals, and the European Union banned the sale of cosmetics tested on animals in 2013. A label that only repeats the law says little.
In many countries, "cruelty-free" has no legal definition, and each brand can use it in its own way. Labels from independent certifiers are more reliable than brands' own claims.

It's true that animal testing causes suffering, that avoiding it is an important step, and that the cruelty-free movement helped pass laws like Brazil's in 2025.
But the label is about testing, not ingredients. For a product to be truly free of cruelty, it also needs to be vegan.
